title: Biochemistry, Cell Biology and Genetics
topics: Cell signalling and the cell cycle

notes.h: Eukaryotic cell structure: organelles and the cytoskeleton
notes.body:
Eukaryotic cells divide work between membrane-bound compartments. Knowing what each organelle does, and which diseases follow when it fails, is the core of this topic.

- Nucleus: double nuclear envelope continuous with the rough ER, perforated by nuclear pore complexes. The nucleolus transcribes rRNA and assembles ribosomal subunits. Nuclear lamins (intermediate filaments) support the envelope; LMNA mutations cause laminopathies such as progeria.
- Ribosomes: eukaryotic 80S (60S + 40S); bacterial 70S (50S + 30S). Svedberg units are not additive. The difference is the basis of selective antibiotic toxicity.
- Rough ER: ribosomes bound via the signal recognition particle make secretory, membrane and lysosomal proteins, translocated during translation. Disulphide bonding and N-linked glycosylation begin here.
- Smooth ER: lipid and steroid synthesis, cytochrome P450 drug metabolism (abundant in hepatocytes), and Ca²⁺ storage (the sarcoplasmic reticulum in muscle).
- Golgi apparatus: modifies and sorts proteins from its cis to its trans face. Lysosomal enzymes receive a mannose-6-phosphate tag that directs them to lysosomes.
- Lysosomes: acid hydrolases at pH about 4.5–5, maintained by a V-type H⁺-ATPase. Enzyme defects cause lysosomal storage disorders.
- Peroxisomes: β-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids, catalase breakdown of H₂O₂, and plasmalogen synthesis. Defective biogenesis causes Zellweger spectrum disorders.
- Mitochondria: double membrane, cristae carrying the respiratory chain, and a circular genome of about 16.6 kb encoding 13 respiratory-chain polypeptides, 22 tRNAs and 2 rRNAs. Inherited maternally. Release of cytochrome c triggers intrinsic apoptosis.

Cytoskeleton
- Microfilaments (actin, about 7 nm): cell shape, cytokinesis, microvilli, muscle contraction with myosin.
- Intermediate filaments (about 10 nm): tissue-specific (keratins in epithelia, vimentin in mesenchyme, desmin in muscle, GFAP in astrocytes, neurofilaments in neurones), so they are used in tumour immunohistochemistry.
- Microtubules (α/β-tubulin, about 25 nm): mitotic spindle and axonal transport. Kinesins move cargo towards the plus end, dyneins towards the minus end. Motile cilia have a 9+2 axoneme (primary cilia 9+0), centrioles nine triplets. Drugs: colchicine and vinca alkaloids block polymerisation; taxanes stabilise microtubules.

Applied illustration
I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II) is caused by deficiency of the Golgi phosphotransferase (GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase) that makes the first step of the mannose-6-phosphate tag. Lysosomal enzymes are secreted instead of delivered, so plasma enzyme levels are high while cells fill with undigested material (inclusion bodies). Primary ciliary dyskinesia (dynein arm defects) causes bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis and subfertility, with situs inversus in about half of cases (Kartagener syndrome).

Exam pitfalls
- Peroxisomes, not lysosomes, start very-long-chain fatty acid oxidation.
- Most mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded, so not every mitochondrial disease is maternally inherited.
- Do not add Svedberg values: 60S + 40S gives 80S, not 100S.

The fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972) describes a phospholipid bilayer in which proteins float and diffuse laterally. Cholesterol buffers fluidity: it stiffens the membrane at high temperature and stops tight packing at low temperature. The two leaflets differ. Phosphatidylserine normally faces the cytosol; in apoptosis it flips outwards as an 'eat me' signal, which annexin V binding detects.

Modes of transport
- Simple diffusion: small non-polar molecules (O₂, CO₂, steroids) move down their gradient. Rate follows Fick's law: proportional to area and concentration gradient, inversely proportional to thickness.
- Facilitated diffusion: channels or carriers (for example GLUT transporters) move solutes down their gradient without ATP. Carriers saturate, giving Michaelis–Menten-like kinetics.
- Primary active transport uses ATP directly. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP, so it is electrogenic; cardiac glycosides such as digoxin inhibit it. Other examples are the Ca²⁺-ATPases (SERCA) and the gastric H⁺/K⁺-ATPase, the target of proton pump inhibitors.
- Secondary active transport uses the Na⁺ gradient: SGLT1 in the gut and SGLT2 in the proximal tubule (the target of SGLT2 inhibitors), and the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger.
- ABC transporters: P-glycoprotein (multidrug resistance) and CFTR, an ABC-family protein that works as a chloride channel.
- Vesicular transport: receptor-mediated endocytosis via clathrin-coated pits (for example LDL uptake via the LDL receptor), and exocytosis.

Membrane potential
The Nernst equation gives each ion's equilibrium potential: E = (RT/zF) ln([out]/[in]). At 37 °C this is about (61.5/z) log₁₀([out]/[in]) mV. Resting potential lies close to E_K because resting membranes are most permeable to K⁺. The Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz equation weights each ion by its permeability.

Worked example
K⁺ is 4 mM outside and 140 mM inside. E_K = 61.5 × log₁₀(4/140) = 61.5 × (−1.544) ≈ −95 mV. If plasma K⁺ rises, the ratio and so E_K move towards zero, and the cell depolarises. This is why hyperkalaemia is arrhythmogenic.

Clinical links
- Cystic fibrosis: CFTR mutations; the commonest, F508del, misfolds and is degraded in the ER (a processing defect). CFTR modulators (correctors and potentiators) target specific classes of defect.
- Nephrogenic and cranial diabetes insipidus (now also termed arginine vasopressin resistance and deficiency): ADH acts on V2 receptors to insert aquaporin-2 into the collecting duct.
- Familial hypercholesterolaemia: defective LDL-receptor endocytosis.

Exam pitfalls
- The Na⁺/K⁺ pump directly contributes only a few millivolts to resting potential. It mainly maintains the gradients that K⁺ leak then uses.
- Facilitated diffusion is saturable and specific but needs no energy.
- Secondary active transport uses ATP indirectly, through the Na⁺ gradient.

notes.h: Protein structure, haemoglobin and enzyme kinetics
notes.body:
Protein structure
- Primary: amino acid sequence joined by planar, rigid peptide bonds.
- Secondary: α-helices and β-pleated sheets held by backbone hydrogen bonds.
- Tertiary: 3D fold stabilised by hydrophobic interactions, ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds and disulphide bridges.
- Quaternary: assembly of subunits, for example haemoglobin (α₂β₂).
Chaperones assist folding. Misfolded proteins can aggregate as amyloid, which has a cross-β-sheet structure.

Haemoglobin
Haemoglobin binds O₂ cooperatively, giving a sigmoidal dissociation curve; myoglobin's curve is hyperbolic. A right shift lowers affinity and aids unloading. Causes are raised CO₂, H⁺ (the Bohr effect), temperature and 2,3-BPG. HbF binds 2,3-BPG poorly, so it has higher O₂ affinity and draws O₂ across the placenta. Carbon monoxide binds haem avidly and shifts the curve left.

Enzymes
Enzymes lower activation energy. They do not change ΔG or the position of equilibrium.
- Michaelis–Menten: v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]). Km is the substrate concentration giving half Vmax.
- Lineweaver–Burk: 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax. The y-intercept is 1/Vmax and the x-intercept is −1/Km.

Inhibition
- Competitive: binds the active site; apparent Km rises, Vmax is unchanged; overcome by excess substrate. Examples: methotrexate (dihydrofolate reductase), statins (HMG-CoA reductase).
- Non-competitive: binds elsewhere; Vmax falls, Km is unchanged.
- Uncompetitive: binds only the ES complex; both Km and Vmax fall.
- Irreversible: aspirin acetylates cyclo-oxygenase; organophosphates inactivate acetylcholinesterase.

Regulation
Allosteric enzymes show sigmoidal kinetics (for example PFK-1 and aspartate transcarbamoylase). Other mechanisms are reversible phosphorylation, zymogen activation (enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen, and trypsin then activates the other pancreatic proenzymes), and induction or repression of synthesis. Many coenzymes come from B vitamins: thiamine pyrophosphate (B1) for pyruvate dehydrogenase and transketolase, pyridoxal phosphate (B6) for transaminases, FAD and NAD⁺ from B2 and B3.

Worked example
An enzyme has Km = 2 mM and Vmax = 100 µmol/min. At [S] = 2 mM, v = 100 × 2/4 = 50 µmol/min. At [S] = 6 mM, v = 100 × 6/8 = 75 µmol/min. Tripling [S] raises the rate by only 50%, because the enzyme is approaching saturation. If a competitive inhibitor doubles the apparent Km to 4 mM, v at 6 mM becomes 100 × 6/10 = 60 µmol/min.

Exam pitfalls
- A low Km means high apparent affinity, but Km is not strictly a dissociation constant.
- Allosteric enzymes do not obey Michaelis–Menten kinetics.
- Enzymes speed up reactions in both directions.

Glycolysis (cytosol)
Glucose is converted to 2 pyruvate, with net yields of 2 ATP and 2 NADH. Three irreversible steps are regulated:
- Hexokinase is inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate. The liver and β-cell isoform, glucokinase, has a high Km and is not inhibited by G6P, so it works as a glucose sensor.
- PFK-1 is the main control point. AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate activate it; ATP and citrate inhibit it.
- Pyruvate kinase. Its deficiency causes haemolytic anaemia, because red cells lack mitochondria and depend on glycolysis.
Under anaerobic conditions, lactate dehydrogenase regenerates NAD⁺ by reducing pyruvate to lactate.

Link reaction and Krebs cycle (mitochondrial matrix)
Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA. It is irreversible and needs thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoate, CoA, FAD and NAD⁺. Thiamine deficiency, seen in alcohol misuse, impairs PDH and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Each turn of the Krebs cycle yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP and 2 CO₂.

Oxidative phosphorylation
Complexes I–IV pass electrons to O₂ and pump protons. ATP synthase uses the proton-motive force (Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory, 1961). Approximate P/O ratios are 2.5 per NADH and 1.5 per FADH₂.
- Inhibitors: rotenone (complex I), cyanide and carbon monoxide (complex IV), oligomycin (ATP synthase).
- Uncouplers such as 2,4-dinitrophenol, and UCP1 (thermogenin) in brown fat, dissipate the gradient as heat.

Worked example: ATP per glucose
- Glycolysis: 2 ATP, plus 2 NADH worth 3 or 5 ATP depending on the shuttle (glycerol-3-phosphate or malate–aspartate)
- PDH: 2 NADH, 5 ATP
- Krebs cycle: 6 NADH (15 ATP), 2 FADH₂ (3 ATP) and 2 GTP (2 ATP)
- Total: about 30–32 ATP

Gluconeogenesis (liver and kidney)
Four enzymes bypass the irreversible glycolytic steps: pyruvate carboxylase (mitochondrial, biotin-dependent), PEP carboxykinase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase. Substrates are lactate (Cori cycle), alanine, glycerol and propionyl-CoA. Even-chain fatty acids cannot make net glucose, because PDH is irreversible.

Glycogen
Glycogen synthase is activated by insulin. Glycogen phosphorylase is activated by glucagon (in liver) and adrenaline, via cAMP and PKA. Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so its glycogen fuels only the muscle itself.
- Von Gierke disease (type I, glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency): fasting hypoglycaemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia, hepatomegaly.
- McArdle disease (type V, muscle phosphorylase deficiency): exercise intolerance, cramps, myoglobinuria.

Pentose phosphate pathway
This pathway makes NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate; G6PD is its rate-limiting enzyme. Red cells need NADPH to keep glutathione reduced. In G6PD deficiency (X-linked), oxidant stress from fava beans, infection, or drugs such as primaquine, dapsone and some sulfonamides causes haemolysis, with Heinz bodies and bite cells.

Exam pitfalls
- 'Net 2 ATP' from glycolysis is after the 2 ATP invested.
- Glucokinase is not product-inhibited.
- Muscle glycogen cannot raise blood glucose.

Fatty acid synthesis (cytosol, fed state)
Acetyl-CoA leaves mitochondria as citrate. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (biotin-dependent, rate-limiting) makes malonyl-CoA. It is activated by citrate and insulin, and inhibited by AMPK phosphorylation. Fatty acid synthase uses NADPH (from the pentose phosphate pathway and malic enzyme) to build palmitate (C16).

β-oxidation (mitochondria, fasting)
Long-chain fatty acids enter via the carnitine shuttle. CPT-I is inhibited by malonyl-CoA, which stops newly made fat being oxidised at once. Each cycle yields 1 FADH₂, 1 NADH and 1 acetyl-CoA.

Worked example: palmitate
Seven cycles give 8 acetyl-CoA (80 ATP), 7 FADH₂ (10.5 ATP) and 7 NADH (17.5 ATP), totalling 108. Activation costs the equivalent of 2 ATP (ATP → AMP), leaving about 106 ATP.

MCAD deficiency (autosomal recessive, on the UK newborn blood spot screen) causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia during fasting or illness.

Ketogenesis and cholesterol
- Hepatic mitochondria make acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate via HMG-CoA synthase during fasting and insulin deficiency. The liver cannot use ketones because it lacks succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase.
- Cholesterol synthesis: HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting step, inhibited by statins. Low intracellular cholesterol activates SREBP-2, which raises LDL-receptor expression.

Lipoproteins
- Chylomicrons (apoB-48) carry dietary triglyceride. VLDL (apoB-100) carries hepatic triglyceride.
- Lipoprotein lipase, activated by apoC-II, releases fatty acids from both.
- LDL (apoB-100) delivers cholesterol via the LDL receptor. HDL (apoA-I) performs reverse cholesterol transport, using LCAT to esterify cholesterol.

Amino acid catabolism
- Transamination (ALT, AST; pyridoxal phosphate) funnels amino groups to glutamate. Glutamate dehydrogenase then releases NH₄⁺.
- Urea cycle (liver): CPS-I and ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) work in mitochondria, the remaining steps in the cytosol. CPS-I requires N-acetylglutamate.
- OTC deficiency is X-linked and the commonest urea cycle disorder. It causes hyperammonaemia with raised urinary orotic acid.
- Carbon skeletons are glucogenic (yield pyruvate or Krebs intermediates) or ketogenic (yield acetyl-CoA or acetoacetate). Leucine and lysine are purely ketogenic.

Inborn errors
- Phenylketonuria: phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency (or a tetrahydrobiopterin defect). Detected on the newborn screen and treated with a lifelong low-phenylalanine diet. Maternal PKU harms the fetus.
- Maple syrup urine disease: branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency.
- Homocystinuria: cystathionine β-synthase deficiency. Lens dislocation (typically downward), thrombosis and a marfanoid habitus.
- Alkaptonuria: homogentisate oxidase deficiency. Urine darkens on standing, with ochronosis and arthropathy.

Exam pitfalls
- Malonyl-CoA links synthesis to oxidation, so the two do not run at the same time.
- Ketone bodies are a normal fasting fuel; ketoacidosis needs severe insulin deficiency.
- Lens dislocation is upward in Marfan syndrome and downward in homocystinuria.

notes.h: DNA replication, repair, transcription and translation
notes.body:
DNA structure and replication
DNA is an antiparallel double helix (Watson and Crick, 1953). A pairs with T by two hydrogen bonds, and G pairs with C by three. Replication is semiconservative (Meselson and Stahl, 1958) and runs 5′→3′ from many origins:
- Helicase unwinds the helix; topoisomerases relieve supercoiling.
- Primase lays RNA primers; DNA polymerases (ε mainly on the leading strand, δ on the lagging) extend them.
- The lagging strand is made as Okazaki fragments, which DNA ligase joins.
- Telomerase, a reverse transcriptase carrying its own RNA template, extends chromosome ends in germ cells, stem cells and most cancers.
Drug targets: fluoroquinolones inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; etoposide (topoisomerase II) and irinotecan (topoisomerase I) are anticancer drugs.

DNA repair
- Mismatch repair (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2): defects cause Lynch syndrome and microsatellite instability.
- Nucleotide excision repair removes bulky lesions such as UV pyrimidine dimers; defects cause xeroderma pigmentosum.
- Base excision repair deals with deaminated, oxidised or alkylated bases.
- Double-strand breaks: homologous recombination (BRCA1, BRCA2) is accurate; non-homologous end joining is error-prone. PARP inhibitors exploit homologous recombination deficiency through synthetic lethality.

Transcription
- RNA polymerase II makes mRNA; polymerase I makes most rRNA; polymerase III makes tRNA and 5S rRNA.
- General transcription factors bind promoter elements such as the TATA box; enhancers and silencers act at a distance.
- Pre-mRNA processing: a 5′ 7-methylguanosine cap, a 3′ poly(A) tail, and splicing of introns by the spliceosome (snRNPs). Alternative splicing gives several proteins from one gene.
- Epigenetics: CpG methylation silences promoters; histone acetylation opens chromatin.

Translation
The code is triplet, degenerate, non-overlapping and almost universal. AUG (methionine) starts translation; UAA, UAG and UGA stop it. The ribosome has three sites: aminoacyl-tRNA enters at the A site, the growing chain is held at the P site, and empty tRNA leaves from the E site. Antibiotics exploit 70S ribosomes: aminoglycosides and tetracyclines act on the 30S subunit; macrolides, chloramphenicol and linezolid act on the 50S.

Worked example
Template strand 3′-TAC GGA TTT-5′ gives mRNA 5′-AUG CCU AAA-3′, which is translated as Met–Pro–Lys. The coding strand has the same sequence as the mRNA, with T in place of U.

Mutations
- Silent, missense, nonsense, frameshift and splice-site mutations.
- Sickle cell disease is a missense change in β-globin: codon 6 GAG → GTG, glutamate to valine.

Exam pitfalls
- Confusing the template and coding strands.
- Forgetting that nucleic acids are always built 5′→3′.
- An in-frame deletion such as F508del removes one amino acid. It does not cause a frameshift.

notes.h: Cell signalling, the cell cycle and apoptosis
notes.body:
Receptor classes
- Ligand-gated ion channels, for example nicotinic acetylcholine and GABA-A receptors: millisecond responses.
- G protein-coupled receptors (seven transmembrane domains):
- Gs activates adenylyl cyclase, so cAMP rises and protein kinase A is activated.
- Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase.
- Gq activates phospholipase C-β, which cleaves PIP₂ into IP₃ (releases Ca²⁺ from the ER) and DAG (activates protein kinase C).
- Signals end when Gα hydrolyses its GTP and phosphodiesterases break down cAMP.
- Receptor tyrosine kinases (insulin receptor, EGFR, HER2): dimerisation and autophosphorylation recruit adaptors, activating the Ras–MAPK and PI3K–Akt pathways. Ras is a small GTPase, active when GTP-bound. Oncogenic Ras mutations impair GTP hydrolysis, so Ras stays switched on.
- Cytokine receptors use associated JAK kinases and STAT transcription factors. The JAK2 V617F mutation drives most cases of polycythaemia vera.
- Intracellular receptors for steroid and thyroid hormones act as ligand-activated transcription factors: slow onset, long duration.

Applied illustration: bacterial toxins
- Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gsα and blocks its GTPase. cAMP stays high in enterocytes, CFTR opens, and Cl⁻ and water are secreted, causing profuse watery diarrhoea.
- Pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates Gi and prevents its activation, which removes the brake on adenylyl cyclase.

The cell cycle
The phases are G1, S (DNA synthesis), G2 and M; G0 is quiescence. Cyclin–CDK complexes drive progression:
- At the G1/S restriction point, cyclin D–CDK4/6 phosphorylates Rb, releasing E2F to switch on S-phase genes. Hypophosphorylated Rb is the active, growth-suppressing form.
- Checkpoints act at G1/S and G2/M (DNA damage) and in metaphase (the spindle assembly checkpoint).
- p53 senses DNA damage and induces p21, a CDK inhibitor that causes arrest. If damage is severe, p53 triggers apoptosis through pro-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins such as BAX and PUMA. MDM2 targets p53 for degradation.

Apoptosis
- Intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway: BAX and BAK permeabilise the outer membrane, cytochrome c is released, the apoptosome forms and caspase-9 is activated. BCL-2 opposes this.
- Extrinsic pathway: Fas ligand or TNF binds a death receptor, FADD is recruited and caspase-8 is activated.
- Both converge on the executioner caspases 3 and 7.

Cancer links and drugs
- Oncogenes act dominantly; tumour suppressors need two hits (Knudson, 1971, from retinoblastoma).
- Targeted drugs: imatinib (BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor), trastuzumab (anti-HER2 antibody), CDK4/6 inhibitors such as palbociclib (hormone receptor-positive breast cancer), and EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma).

Exam pitfalls
- Ras is not a receptor.
- Phosphorylating Rb inactivates it.
- cAMP activates PKA; DAG activates PKC.
- Steroid receptors are mostly intracellular.

notes.h: Patterns of inheritance and medical genetics
notes.body:
Mendelian patterns
- Autosomal dominant: affected individuals in every generation, a 50% risk to each child, and male-to-male transmission possible. Penetrance may be incomplete and expressivity variable. Examples: Huntington disease, Marfan syndrome, NF1, familial hypercholesterolaemia, ADPKD, BRCA1/2 predisposition.
- Autosomal recessive: affected siblings with unaffected parents, a 25% risk when both parents are carriers, and more common with consanguinity. Examples: cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease, β-thalassaemia, PKU, HFE haemochromatosis, most inborn errors of metabolism.
- X-linked recessive: mostly males affected, no male-to-male transmission, and all daughters of an affected male are carriers. Examples: Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy, haemophilia A and B, G6PD deficiency. Female carriers can show signs through skewed X-inactivation (lyonisation).
- X-linked dominant: an affected father passes the condition to all his daughters and none of his sons. Example: X-linked hypophosphataemia.
- Mitochondrial: transmitted only through the mother. Heteroplasmy gives variable severity. Examples: MELAS, Leber hereditary optic neuropathy.

Non-classical mechanisms
- Repeat expansions with anticipation (earlier onset or greater severity in successive generations): Huntington (CAG, worse through the father), myotonic dystrophy type 1 (CTG, congenital form through the mother), and fragile X (CGG in FMR1, expansion through the mother). Friedreich ataxia (intronic GAA expansion in FXN, autosomal recessive) is also a repeat disorder, but anticipation is not a typical feature.
- Genomic imprinting: a 15q11–q13 deletion on the paternal chromosome causes Prader–Willi syndrome; on the maternal chromosome (or loss of UBE3A) it causes Angelman syndrome. Uniparental disomy can produce the same picture.
- Mosaicism, including gonadal mosaicism, explains recurrence after an apparently new mutation.

Hardy–Weinberg
For two alleles, p + q = 1 and genotype frequencies are p² + 2pq + q². This assumes random mating and no selection, mutation or migration in a large population.

Worked example
Cystic fibrosis affects about 1 in 2,500 births in people of northern European ancestry. q² = 1/2,500, so q = 1/50, and the carrier frequency 2pq ≈ 2 × (1/50) × (49/50) ≈ 1 in 25. An unaffected sibling of an affected child has a 2/3 chance of being a carrier, because the affected genotype is excluded. If that sibling has a child with an unrelated partner, the risk the child is affected is 2/3 × 1/25 × 1/4 = 1/150.

Testing in the NHS
- Karyotype, FISH and chromosomal microarray (detects copy-number variants).
- Targeted gene panels and whole-genome sequencing, organised through the NHS Genomic Medicine Service and the National Genomic Test Directory.
- The newborn blood spot screen covers PKU, MCAD deficiency, cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease and congenital hypothyroidism, among others.

Exam pitfalls
- Penetrance (whether a phenotype appears at all) is not expressivity (how severe it is).
- Carrier risk for an unaffected sibling is 2/3, not 1/2.
- Mitochondrial disease can come from nuclear genes as well as mtDNA.

cards.f: Which organelle carries out β-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids?
cards.b: The peroxisome. Its products are then passed to mitochondria to finish oxidation. Defective peroxisome biogenesis (Zellweger spectrum) causes very-long-chain fatty acids to build up.

cards.f: What tag targets newly made enzymes to the lysosome, and where is it added?
cards.b: Mannose-6-phosphate, added in the cis-Golgi. M6P receptors in the trans-Golgi then sort the enzymes into vesicles bound for lysosomes.

cards.f: Explain the biochemical basis of I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II).
cards.b: GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase is deficient, so lysosomal enzymes get no M6P tag and are secreted. Plasma enzyme levels are high, while lysosomes fill with undigested material.

cards.f: Compare eukaryotic and prokaryotic ribosome sizes.
cards.b: Eukaryotic: 80S (60S + 40S). Prokaryotic: 70S (50S + 30S). Svedberg units are not additive, and the difference lets antibiotics target bacteria selectively.

cards.f: Name four intermediate filament proteins and the cell types that express them.
cards.b: Cytokeratins (epithelium), vimentin (mesenchyme), desmin (muscle), GFAP (astrocytes); neurofilaments (neurones) are a fifth. Their tissue specificity helps classify tumours by immunohistochemistry.

cards.f: Which motor protein moves cargo towards the minus end of microtubules, and what happens when it fails in cilia?
cards.b: Dynein. Defective axonemal dynein arms cause primary ciliary dyskinesia: bronchiectasis, sinusitis and subfertility, with situs inversus in about half of patients (Kartagener syndrome).

cards.f: How do taxanes and vinca alkaloids differ in their action on microtubules?
cards.b: Vinca alkaloids (and colchicine) block tubulin polymerisation. Taxanes stabilise microtubules and stop them depolymerising. Either way the mitotic spindle fails and cells arrest in M phase.

cards.f: What does the mitochondrial genome encode?
cards.b: A circular genome of about 16.6 kb encoding 13 respiratory-chain polypeptides, 22 tRNAs and 2 rRNAs. Most mitochondrial proteins are encoded in the nucleus and imported.

cards.f: Why are hepatocytes rich in smooth endoplasmic reticulum?
cards.b: Smooth ER houses the cytochrome P450 enzymes for drug and xenobiotic metabolism, and enzymes for lipid and steroid synthesis. Drugs that induce P450 expand it.

cards.f: What do mutations in LMNA cause, and why?
cards.b: Laminopathies, such as Hutchinson–Gilford progeria and some muscular dystrophies and cardiomyopathies. Lamin A/C is an intermediate filament of the nuclear lamina, and defects destabilise the nuclear envelope.

cards.f: State the stoichiometry of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase.
cards.b: Per ATP hydrolysed it pumps 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in. The net outward movement of positive charge makes it electrogenic.

cards.f: How does cholesterol affect membrane fluidity?
cards.b: It buffers fluidity. At high temperature it restrains phospholipid movement, so fluidity falls; at low temperature it stops tight packing, so fluidity is kept up.

cards.f: Give the Nernst equation and its simplified form at 37 °C.
cards.b: E = (RT/zF) ln([out]/[in]). At 37 °C this is about (61.5/z) log₁₀([out]/[in]) mV.

cards.f: Distinguish primary from secondary active transport, with an example of each.
cards.b: Primary active transport hydrolyses ATP directly, as in the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Secondary active transport uses a gradient set up by a primary pump; SGLT2 couples glucose uptake to Na⁺ entry.

cards.f: Why does F508del CFTR fail to reach the apical membrane?
cards.b: Deleting phenylalanine 508 misfolds the protein. ER quality control retains it and sends it for proteasomal degradation, so it is a class II (processing) defect.

cards.f: Which features distinguish carrier-mediated facilitated diffusion from simple diffusion?
cards.b: It is saturable (shows a Vmax), specific, and can be competitively inhibited. Like simple diffusion, it moves solute only down its gradient and needs no energy.

cards.f: Why does the resting membrane potential lie close to E_K?
cards.b: At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K⁺ (via leak channels) than to other ions. The Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz equation weights each ion by its permeability, so K⁺ dominates.

cards.f: What does annexin V binding on a cell surface indicate?
cards.b: Phosphatidylserine has moved to the outer leaflet, an early sign of apoptosis. In healthy cells flippases keep it on the inner leaflet.

cards.f: How does ADH increase water reabsorption in the collecting duct?
cards.b: It binds V2 receptors (Gs-coupled), raising cAMP. PKA then drives aquaporin-2 vesicles to insert into the apical membrane.

cards.f: Which membrane protein is the target of proton pump inhibitors?
cards.b: The H⁺/K⁺-ATPase of gastric parietal cells, a P-type primary active pump. PPIs bind it irreversibly.

cards.f: Define Km.
cards.b: The substrate concentration at which the reaction rate is half of Vmax. A low Km means high apparent affinity of the enzyme for its substrate.

cards.f: How does a competitive inhibitor change Km and Vmax?
cards.b: Apparent Km rises; Vmax is unchanged. On a Lineweaver–Burk plot the lines cross at the y-axis.

cards.f: How does a non-competitive inhibitor change Km and Vmax?
cards.b: Vmax falls; Km is unchanged. The inhibitor binds away from the active site, and raising [S] cannot overcome it. The lines cross on the x-axis.

cards.f: What are the intercepts of a Lineweaver–Burk plot?
cards.b: The y-intercept is 1/Vmax, the x-intercept is −1/Km, and the slope is Km/Vmax.

cards.f: List four factors that shift the haemoglobin–O₂ dissociation curve to the right.
cards.b: Raised CO₂, raised H⁺ (lower pH, the Bohr effect), raised temperature and raised 2,3-BPG. Each lowers O₂ affinity and aids unloading in tissues.

cards.f: Why does fetal haemoglobin have higher O₂ affinity than adult haemoglobin?
cards.b: HbF (α₂γ₂) binds 2,3-BPG poorly, because the γ chain lacks a key positive residue in the binding pocket. Its curve lies to the left, so it takes O₂ from maternal blood.

cards.f: How does aspirin inhibit cyclo-oxygenase?
cards.b: It irreversibly acetylates a serine in the active site of COX-1 and COX-2. Platelets have no nucleus and cannot make new enzyme, so the effect lasts for the platelet's lifespan.

cards.f: Which coenzyme do transaminases such as ALT and AST need, and from which vitamin does it come?
cards.b: Pyridoxal phosphate, from vitamin B6.

cards.f: Why do allosteric enzymes give sigmoidal rather than hyperbolic kinetics?
cards.b: Their subunits show cooperativity: binding at one site changes the affinity of the others, typically switching between T and R states. They do not follow Michaelis–Menten kinetics.

cards.f: What is the secondary structure of amyloid fibrils?
cards.b: Cross-β-pleated sheet. This structure gives apple-green birefringence under polarised light after Congo red staining.

cards.f: What is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis, and what are its main regulators?
cards.b: Phosphofructokinase-1. AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate activate it; ATP and citrate inhibit it.

cards.f: Why is glucokinase suited to the liver and pancreatic β-cell?
cards.b: It has a high Km and is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate. Its activity therefore tracks blood glucose across the physiological range, so it works as a glucose sensor.

cards.f: Name the four enzymes unique to gluconeogenesis.
cards.b: Pyruvate carboxylase, PEP carboxykinase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase.

cards.f: Why can't even-chain fatty acids be converted into net glucose?
cards.b: They yield only acetyl-CoA. PDH is irreversible, and both acetyl carbons are lost as CO₂ in the Krebs cycle, so no net oxaloacetate is made.

cards.f: What is the site of action of cyanide in the respiratory chain?
cards.b: Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), at the ferric haem a₃. Electron transfer to O₂ stops, oxidative phosphorylation halts and lactic acidosis follows.

cards.f: How do uncouplers such as 2,4-dinitrophenol cause hyperthermia?
cards.b: They carry protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, bypassing ATP synthase. Electron transport speeds up but the gradient is lost as heat instead of being used to make ATP.

cards.f: Give the features of von Gierke disease.
cards.b: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (GSD type I): severe fasting hypoglycaemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia, hyperlipidaemia and hepatomegaly.

cards.f: Why does G6PD deficiency cause haemolysis under oxidant stress?
cards.b: G6PD makes NADPH, which red cells need to keep glutathione reduced. Without it, oxidants denature haemoglobin (Heinz bodies) and damage membranes.

cards.f: Which cofactors does pyruvate dehydrogenase require?
cards.b: Thiamine pyrophosphate (B1), lipoic acid, coenzyme A (B5), FAD (B2) and NAD⁺ (B3).

cards.f: Why can't muscle glycogen raise blood glucose?
cards.b: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase. Glucose-6-phosphate from glycogen stays inside the muscle and enters glycolysis.

cards.f: What is the rate-limiting enzyme of fatty acid synthesis, and how is it regulated?
cards.b: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (biotin-dependent). Citrate and insulin activate it; AMPK phosphorylation, glucagon and long-chain acyl-CoA inhibit it.

cards.f: How does malonyl-CoA stop fatty acid synthesis and oxidation running at the same time?
cards.b: It inhibits CPT-I, so fatty acids cannot enter mitochondria for β-oxidation while synthesis is active.

cards.f: Why can't the liver use the ketone bodies it makes?
cards.b: It lacks succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase (thiophorase), which converts acetoacetate to acetoacetyl-CoA.

cards.f: Which apolipoprotein activates lipoprotein lipase?
cards.b: ApoC-II. Its deficiency, like lipoprotein lipase deficiency, causes severe hypertriglyceridaemia (familial chylomicronaemia syndrome).

cards.f: How do statins lower LDL cholesterol?
cards.b: They competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase. Hepatic cholesterol falls, SREBP-2 is activated and LDL-receptor expression rises, so more LDL is cleared from plasma.

cards.f: Which urea cycle disorder is X-linked, and what biochemical marker helps distinguish it?
cards.b: Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency. Unused carbamoyl phosphate spills into pyrimidine synthesis, so urinary orotic acid rises.

cards.f: Name the two purely ketogenic amino acids.
cards.b: Leucine and lysine.

cards.f: Give the enzyme defect and main features of classical homocystinuria.
cards.b: Cystathionine β-synthase deficiency: lens dislocation (typically downward), marfanoid habitus, learning disability and arterial and venous thrombosis.

cards.f: What is MCAD deficiency, and how does it present?
cards.b: An autosomal recessive defect of medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase in β-oxidation. It causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia during fasting or illness and is on the UK newborn blood spot screen.

cards.f: What are the net ATP yields from complete oxidation of palmitate?
cards.b: About 106 ATP: 108 from 8 acetyl-CoA, 7 FADH₂ and 7 NADH, minus 2 ATP equivalents for activation.

cards.f: What does 'semiconservative replication' mean, and which experiment showed it?
cards.b: Each daughter duplex contains one parental and one new strand. Meselson and Stahl (1958) showed it with ¹⁵N/¹⁴N density labelling.

cards.f: Why is the lagging strand made discontinuously?
cards.b: Polymerases synthesise only 5′→3′. The lagging strand template runs the other way, so it is copied in short Okazaki fragments that ligase then joins.

cards.f: Which DNA repair pathway is defective in Lynch syndrome?
cards.b: Mismatch repair (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2), giving microsatellite instability. It predisposes to colorectal, endometrial and other cancers.

cards.f: What is the principle behind PARP inhibitors in BRCA-mutated cancers?
cards.b: Synthetic lethality. Blocking PARP-dependent repair of single-strand breaks creates double-strand breaks that HR-deficient (BRCA) tumour cells cannot repair accurately, so they die. Normal cells survive.

cards.f: List the three main processing steps of eukaryotic pre-mRNA.
cards.b: A 5′ 7-methylguanosine cap, splicing out of introns by the spliceosome, and 3′ polyadenylation.

cards.f: Which RNA polymerase transcribes mRNA in eukaryotes?
cards.b: RNA polymerase II. Pol I makes most rRNA, and Pol III makes tRNA and 5S rRNA.

cards.f: Name antibiotics acting on the 30S and on the 50S bacterial ribosomal subunits.
cards.b: 30S: aminoglycosides and tetracyclines. 50S: macrolides, chloramphenicol, clindamycin and linezolid.

cards.f: What is the molecular defect in sickle cell disease?
cards.b: A missense mutation in β-globin codon 6 (GAG → GTG) replaces glutamate with valine. Deoxygenated HbS polymerises.

cards.f: Which repair pathway is defective in xeroderma pigmentosum?
cards.b: Nucleotide excision repair, which removes UV-induced pyrimidine dimers. Patients have extreme sun sensitivity and a greatly raised risk of skin cancer.

cards.f: What is telomerase, and why does it matter in cancer?
cards.b: A ribonucleoprotein reverse transcriptase (TERT plus an RNA template) that extends telomeres. Most cancers reactivate it, which lets them divide without limit.

cards.f: Describe the Gq signalling pathway.
cards.b: Gq activates phospholipase C-β, which cleaves PIP₂ into IP₃ and DAG. IP₃ releases Ca²⁺ from the ER; DAG with Ca²⁺ activates protein kinase C.

cards.f: How does cholera toxin cause secretory diarrhoea?
cards.b: It ADP-ribosylates Gsα and blocks its GTPase, so adenylyl cyclase stays active. High cAMP opens CFTR, and Cl⁻ and water are secreted into the gut lumen.

cards.f: What type of protein is Ras, and how do oncogenic mutations affect it?
cards.b: A small monomeric GTPase that relays RTK signals to the MAPK pathway. Oncogenic mutations (for example at codon 12) impair GTP hydrolysis, so Ras stays active.

cards.f: What is the function of Rb at the G1/S checkpoint?
cards.b: Hypophosphorylated Rb binds E2F and blocks transcription of S-phase genes. Cyclin D–CDK4/6 (then cyclin E–CDK2) phosphorylates Rb, releasing E2F.

cards.f: How does p53 cause cell-cycle arrest after DNA damage?
cards.b: Stabilised p53 transcribes p21 (CDKN1A), which inhibits cyclin–CDK complexes. Arrest happens at G1/S, giving time for repair.

cards.f: Outline the intrinsic pathway of apoptosis.
cards.b: BAX and BAK permeabilise the outer mitochondrial membrane. Cytochrome c is released and binds Apaf-1 to form the apoptosome, which activates caspase-9 and then caspases 3 and 7.

cards.f: Which signalling pathway do cytokine receptors such as the EPO receptor use?
cards.b: JAK–STAT. Receptor-associated JAKs phosphorylate STATs, which dimerise and enter the nucleus to act as transcription factors.

cards.f: Where are steroid hormone receptors found, and how do they act?
cards.b: Mostly in the cytoplasm or nucleus. When ligand binds, they act as transcription factors on hormone response elements, so effects are slow in onset and long-lasting.

cards.f: What is Knudson's two-hit hypothesis?
cards.b: Both alleles of a tumour suppressor must be inactivated before a tumour forms. In inherited retinoblastoma the first hit is in the germline, so tumours arise earlier and are often bilateral (Knudson, 1971).

cards.f: Give a targeted drug for each: BCR-ABL, HER2, CDK4/6.
cards.b: Imatinib (tyrosine kinase inhibitor), trastuzumab (monoclonal antibody) and palbociclib (CDK4/6 inhibitor).

cards.f: Distinguish penetrance from expressivity.
cards.b: Penetrance is the proportion of people with a genotype who show any phenotype. Expressivity is the range of severity among those who do.

cards.f: What is the chance that an unaffected sibling of a child with an autosomal recessive disease is a carrier?
cards.b: 2/3. Of the three remaining genotypes (AA, Aa, aA), two are carriers.

cards.f: State the Hardy–Weinberg equation and its assumptions.
cards.b: p² + 2pq + q² = 1, with p + q = 1. It assumes a large, randomly mating population with no selection, mutation, migration or genetic drift.

cards.f: What is anticipation, and which repeats show it?
cards.b: Earlier onset or greater severity in successive generations, caused by unstable repeat expansion. Examples are Huntington (CAG), myotonic dystrophy type 1 (CTG) and fragile X (CGG).

cards.f: Contrast Prader–Willi and Angelman syndromes genetically.
cards.b: Both involve 15q11–q13. Loss of the paternal contribution causes Prader–Willi; loss of the maternal contribution (UBE3A) causes Angelman. Deletion, uniparental disomy or imprinting defects can cause either.

cards.f: Which pedigree feature excludes X-linked inheritance?
cards.b: Male-to-male transmission, because a father passes his Y chromosome, not his X, to his sons.

cards.f: What is heteroplasmy?
cards.b: A mixture of mutant and normal mitochondrial DNA in a cell. The proportion varies between tissues and offspring, which explains variable severity in mitochondrial disease.

cards.f: How can a female carrier of an X-linked recessive disorder show symptoms?
cards.b: Through skewed X-inactivation (lyonisation), where most cells inactivate the normal X. Rarer causes are Turner syndrome or X-autosome translocations.

cards.f: If an AR disease has incidence 1 in 10,000, what is the carrier frequency?
cards.b: q = √(1/10,000) = 1/100, and 2pq ≈ 2 × 1/100 = 1/50. About 1 in 50 people are carriers.

cards.f: What does chromosomal microarray detect that a standard karyotype misses?
cards.b: Submicroscopic copy-number variants (small deletions and duplications), such as 22q11.2 deletion. It cannot detect balanced translocations.

questions.q: Which organelle is the main site of N-linked glycosylation and translocation of newly made secretory proteins?
questions.why: Ribosomes bound to the rough ER translocate secretory proteins into the lumen during translation, and N-linked glycosylation begins there.

questions.q: Extracellular K⁺ is 4 mM and intracellular K⁺ is 140 mM. Using E = 61.5 log₁₀([out]/[in]) mV, what is E_K at 37 °C?
questions.why: log₁₀(4/140) = −1.544, and 61.5 × −1.544 ≈ −95 mV. The negative sign follows from the higher concentration inside.

questions.q: In the presence of a drug, an enzyme's apparent Km rises while its Vmax is unchanged. Which drug acts in this way on its target enzyme?
questions.why: A raised Km with unchanged Vmax is competitive inhibition; methotrexate competes with folate at DHFR. Aspirin and organophosphates inhibit irreversibly.

questions.q: A 3-year-old has fasting hypoglycaemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia and marked hepatomegaly. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
questions.why: This is von Gierke disease (GSD I). Without glucose-6-phosphatase the liver cannot release free glucose, and G6P is diverted to lactate, urate and lipid.

questions.q: A 2-day-old boy becomes lethargic with vomiting and hyperventilation. Plasma ammonia is very high, plasma citrulline is low, and urinary orotic acid is raised. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
questions.why: Raised orotic acid with low citrulline points to OTC deficiency: carbamoyl phosphate spills into pyrimidine synthesis. In CPS-I deficiency orotic acid is low or normal.

questions.q: Which DNA repair pathway is defective in xeroderma pigmentosum?
questions.why: Nucleotide excision repair removes bulky UV-induced pyrimidine dimers; its loss causes extreme photosensitivity and skin cancers.

questions.q: Which second messenger directly releases Ca²⁺ from the endoplasmic reticulum after a Gq-coupled receptor is activated?
questions.why: IP₃ binds IP₃ receptors on the ER and releases Ca²⁺; DAG stays in the membrane and activates PKC.

questions.q: A couple's first child has cystic fibrosis. Their unaffected daughter, aged 25, asks the chance that she is a carrier. What is it?
questions.why: She cannot be affected, so of the three remaining equally likely genotypes, two are carriers: 2/3.

questions.q: An enzyme has Km = 2 mM and Vmax = 100 µmol/min. A competitive inhibitor raises the apparent Km to 4 mM. What is the rate at [S] = 6 mM with the inhibitor present?
questions.why: v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) = 100 × 6/(4 + 6) = 60 µmol/min. Without the inhibitor it would be 75 µmol/min.

questions.q: Which enzyme is the main rate-limiting control point of glycolysis?
questions.why: PFK-1 catalyses the committed step. It is activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and inhibited by ATP and citrate.

questions.q: Describe the structure and function of the three classes of cytoskeletal filament.
markScheme: Microfilaments: actin, about 7 nm; cell shape, motility, cytokinesis, contraction with myosin
Intermediate filaments: about 10 nm, tissue-specific proteins (keratin, vimentin, desmin, GFAP); mechanical strength
Microtubules: α/β-tubulin, about 25 nm; mitotic spindle, cilia and flagella, intracellular transport
Motor proteins: kinesin moves to the plus end, dynein to the minus end; myosin works on actin
questions.modelAnswer: Microfilaments are thin (about 7 nm) actin polymers. They support cell shape and drive motility, cytokinesis and, with myosin, muscle contraction. Intermediate filaments (about 10 nm) give tensile strength; their proteins are tissue-specific (keratins, vimentin, desmin, GFAP), which helps classify tumours. Microtubules are hollow α/β-tubulin tubes about 25 nm across. They form the mitotic spindle and the axonemes of cilia, and they serve as tracks for transport: kinesins move cargo to the plus end and dyneins to the minus end.

questions.q: Explain why cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) dysfunction causes thick airway secretions, and outline how CFTR modulators work.
markScheme: CFTR is an ABC-family, cAMP/PKA-regulated apical chloride (and bicarbonate) channel
Loss of function reduces Cl⁻ and HCO₃⁻ secretion; Na⁺ absorption via ENaC continues, dehydrating the airway surface liquid
Dehydrated mucus impairs mucociliary clearance, leading to infection and inflammation
Correctors improve folding and trafficking (e.g. F508del); potentiators increase channel opening probability
questions.modelAnswer: CFTR is an apical chloride and bicarbonate channel of the ABC family, opened by cAMP-dependent PKA phosphorylation and ATP binding. When it fails, epithelia secrete less Cl⁻ and HCO₃⁻, while Na⁺ absorption through ENaC continues. Water follows the salt out of the airway, so the surface liquid becomes depleted and the mucus thick and acidic. Cilia cannot clear it, and chronic infection and inflammation lead to bronchiectasis. Modulators work at the protein level. Correctors help misfolded proteins such as F508del fold and reach the membrane. Potentiators increase the time the channel spends open. Combinations are used depending on genotype.

questions.q: Explain why the haemoglobin–oxygen dissociation curve is sigmoidal, whereas myoglobin's is hyperbolic.
markScheme: Haemoglobin is a tetramer with four haem sites; myoglobin is a monomer with one
Cooperative binding: O₂ binding shifts haemoglobin from the low-affinity T state to the high-affinity R state
So affinity rises as saturation increases, giving a sigmoid curve suited to loading in lungs and unloading in tissues
questions.modelAnswer: Myoglobin is a single chain with one haem, so it binds O₂ by simple equilibrium and its curve is hyperbolic. Haemoglobin is an α₂β₂ tetramer. Binding O₂ to one subunit favours a shift from the tense (T) to the relaxed (R) state, which raises the affinity of the remaining sites. This cooperativity gives a steep sigmoid curve. Haemoglobin therefore loads almost fully at alveolar PO₂ and releases a large fraction over the narrow range of PO₂ found in tissues.

questions.q: Calculate the approximate ATP yield from complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule, showing your working. Use P/O ratios of 2.5 for NADH and 1.5 for FADH₂.
markScheme: Glycolysis: net 2 ATP and 2 cytosolic NADH
Cytosolic NADH yields 1.5 or 2.5 ATP each depending on shuttle (glycerol-3-phosphate vs malate–aspartate): 3 or 5 ATP
PDH: 2 NADH = 5 ATP
Krebs cycle (×2): 6 NADH = 15 ATP; 2 FADH₂ = 3 ATP; 2 GTP = 2 ATP
Total about 30–32 ATP
questions.modelAnswer: Glycolysis gives a net 2 ATP and 2 NADH in the cytosol. That NADH enters mitochondria either by the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle, giving FADH₂ (2 × 1.5 = 3 ATP), or by the malate–aspartate shuttle, giving NADH (2 × 2.5 = 5 ATP). Pyruvate dehydrogenase makes 2 NADH, worth 5 ATP. Two turns of the Krebs cycle give 6 NADH (15 ATP), 2 FADH₂ (3 ATP) and 2 GTP (2 ATP). Adding these up: 2 + 3 + 5 + 15 + 3 + 2 = 30 ATP with the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle, or 32 with the malate–aspartate shuttle.

questions.q: Describe how the fed and fasted states regulate fatty acid synthesis and β-oxidation.
markScheme: Fed: insulin dephosphorylates and activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase; citrate allosterically activates it
Malonyl-CoA produced inhibits CPT-I, preventing β-oxidation
Fasting: glucagon and AMPK phosphorylate and inhibit ACC; malonyl-CoA falls
CPT-I is then disinhibited, allowing fatty acid entry into mitochondria for β-oxidation and ketogenesis
questions.modelAnswer: In the fed state insulin promotes dephosphorylation of acetyl-CoA carboxylase, and abundant citrate activates it allosterically. ACC makes malonyl-CoA, which feeds fatty acid synthase and also inhibits CPT-I, so newly made fatty acids are not oxidised straight away. In fasting, glucagon (via PKA) and AMPK phosphorylate and inactivate ACC. Malonyl-CoA falls, CPT-I is released, and long-chain acyl-CoA enters mitochondria for β-oxidation. In the liver the resulting acetyl-CoA supports ketogenesis.

questions.q: A coding-strand DNA sequence reads 5′-ATG GCT TGG AAA-3′. Give the mRNA and the amino acid sequence, and state the effect of mutating the third codon to TGA.
markScheme: mRNA: 5′-AUG GCU UGG AAA-3′ (same as coding strand with U for T)
Peptide: Met–Ala–Trp–Lys
TGG → TGA gives UGA, a stop codon
Nonsense mutation: truncated peptide Met–Ala (and the mRNA is likely degraded by nonsense-mediated decay)
questions.modelAnswer: The mRNA has the same sequence as the coding strand, with uracil in place of thymine: 5′-AUG GCU UGG AAA-3′. Read in frame from AUG, it encodes methionine, alanine, tryptophan and lysine (Met–Ala–Trp–Lys). Changing TGG to TGA turns codon three into UGA, a stop codon. This is a nonsense mutation, so translation would end after Met–Ala. In a full-length gene, a premature stop codon well upstream of the last exon junction usually triggers nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, so little truncated protein is made.

questions.q: Explain how the retinoblastoma protein (Rb) and p53 control the G1/S transition.
markScheme: Hypophosphorylated Rb binds and sequesters E2F, blocking S-phase gene transcription
Mitogen-induced cyclin D–CDK4/6 (then cyclin E–CDK2) phosphorylates Rb, releasing E2F
DNA damage stabilises p53 (escaping MDM2), which transcribes p21
p21 inhibits cyclin–CDK complexes, keeping Rb hypophosphorylated and arresting the cell; severe damage triggers p53-mediated apoptosis
questions.modelAnswer: Rb guards the restriction point. In its hypophosphorylated form it binds the E2F transcription factors and holds back the genes needed for DNA synthesis. Growth factors induce cyclin D, which activates CDK4/6. These kinases, followed by cyclin E–CDK2, phosphorylate Rb and release E2F, committing the cell to S phase. p53 is kept at low levels by MDM2. DNA damage activates kinases such as ATM and ATR, which stabilise p53. p53 then transcribes p21, a CDK inhibitor, so Rb stays unphosphorylated and the cell arrests in G1 while it repairs. If the damage cannot be repaired, p53 induces pro-apoptotic genes such as BAX and PUMA.

questions.q: Using Hardy–Weinberg, a recessive disorder affects 1 in 3,600 births. Calculate the allele frequency and carrier frequency.
markScheme: Carrier frequency 2pq = 2 × 59/60 × 1/60 ≈ 1/30.5 (about 1 in 30)
questions.modelAnswer: The frequency of affected homozygotes is q² = 1/3,600, so the disease allele frequency is q = √(1/3,600) = 1/60. The normal allele frequency is p = 1 − 1/60 = 59/60. The carrier frequency is 2pq = 2 × (59/60) × (1/60) = 118/3,600 ≈ 0.033, or about 1 in 30. Because p is close to 1, 2q gives a good shortcut (2/60 = 1/30). This assumes Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium: random mating and no selection, mutation, migration or drift.

questions.q: Explain, using the Nernst equation, why hyperkalaemia first makes cardiac myocytes more excitable but at higher levels can cause conduction failure and asystole.
markScheme: E_K = 61.5 log₁₀([K⁺]out/[K⁺]in); raising [K⁺]out makes E_K less negative
Resting potential follows E_K, so the membrane depolarises towards threshold, raising excitability
Sustained depolarisation inactivates voltage-gated Na⁺ channels (h-gates close)
Fewer available Na⁺ channels slows phase 0 upstroke and conduction velocity, widening QRS
Severe hyperkalaemia leads to loss of excitability: bradyarrhythmia, sine-wave pattern, VF or asystole
questions.modelAnswer: From the Nernst equation, E_K = 61.5 log₁₀([K⁺]out/[K⁺]in). Raising plasma K⁺ from 4 to 8 mM, with 140 mM inside, moves E_K from about −95 mV to about −76 mV. Resting potential tracks E_K, so cells depolarise towards threshold and at first become more excitable. But sustained depolarisation inactivates voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, which need a negative potential to recover from inactivation. With fewer channels available, the phase 0 upstroke is slower and smaller and conduction slows: the P waves flatten and the QRS widens. At severe levels cells cannot fire at all, giving a sine-wave rhythm, ventricular fibrillation or asystole.

questions.q: Distinguish between a missense, a nonsense and a frameshift mutation, giving a clinical example of each.
markScheme: Missense: single base change altering one amino acid, e.g. sickle cell (β-globin Glu6Val)
Nonsense: change creating a premature stop codon, e.g. many Duchenne muscular dystrophy nonsense variants in DMD
Frameshift: insertion or deletion not divisible by three, shifting the reading frame, e.g. out-of-frame DMD deletions (Duchenne) versus in-frame (Becker)
questions.modelAnswer: A missense mutation changes a single codon so that a different amino acid is inserted. In sickle cell disease, GAG becomes GTG in β-globin, replacing glutamate with valine. A nonsense mutation turns a codon into a premature stop, truncating the protein, as in some Duchenne muscular dystrophy cases. A frameshift results from inserting or deleting a number of bases not divisible by three, so every downstream codon is misread. In DMD, out-of-frame deletions usually cause severe Duchenne disease, whereas in-frame deletions keep a partly functional dystrophin and cause milder Becker disease (the reading-frame rule).

questions.q: Eleanor, a 9-month-old girl, is referred with coarse facial features, gum hypertrophy, restricted joint movement and developmental delay. Her skin fibroblasts contain many inclusion bodies. Plasma activity of several lysosomal hydrolases is markedly raised, whereas activity in her fibroblasts is low. Explain these findings by tracing the normal route of a lysosomal enzyme from synthesis to the lysosome, and identify the most likely defect.
markScheme: Lysosomal hydrolases are synthesised on rough ER ribosomes via a signal peptide and SRP-mediated co-translational translocation
N-linked glycosylation in the ER adds high-mannose oligosaccharides
In the cis-Golgi, GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase recognises lysosomal enzymes and adds GlcNAc-1-phosphate to mannose residues
An uncovering enzyme exposes the mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag
M6P receptors in the trans-Golgi network bind tagged enzymes and package them into clathrin-coated vesicles to late endosomes
Acidic pH in endosomes releases enzymes; receptors are recycled
Diagnosis: I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II), autosomal recessive phosphotransferase deficiency
Without M6P, enzymes enter the default secretory pathway, raising plasma levels
Lysosomes lack hydrolases, so undigested glycosaminoglycans and lipids accumulate as inclusion bodies
Clinical features resemble severe mucopolysaccharidosis; contrast with a single-enzyme storage disease where plasma level of that enzyme is low
questions.modelAnswer:
Lysosomal hydrolases begin like any secretory protein. An N-terminal signal sequence is recognised by the signal recognition particle, and translation continues on the rough ER, with the chain fed into the lumen. There it folds and acquires N-linked high-mannose oligosaccharides.

The key sorting step takes place in the cis-Golgi. GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase recognises a three-dimensional patch shared by lysosomal enzymes and adds N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphate to selected mannose residues. An uncovering enzyme then removes the GlcNAc, exposing mannose-6-phosphate. In the trans-Golgi network, M6P receptors bind the tagged enzymes and concentrate them into clathrin-coated vesicles, which travel to late endosomes. The acidic pH releases the enzymes, the receptors return to the Golgi, and the endosome matures into a lysosome kept at about pH 5 by the V-ATPase.

Eleanor's findings fit I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II), an autosomal recessive deficiency of the phosphotransferase, usually caused by GNPTAB variants. Her enzymes are made normally but never receive the M6P tag. Without it they follow the default constitutive secretory pathway and leave the cell, which explains the high plasma activities alongside low intracellular activity. Her lysosomes therefore lack many hydrolases at once and cannot break down glycosaminoglycans, glycolipids and oligosaccharides. The material builds up as the dense inclusions that give the disease its name.

The multi-enzyme deficit produces a severe phenotype resembling the mucopolysaccharidoses: coarse facies, gingival hypertrophy, skeletal dysplasia, joint contractures and developmental delay. The pattern is distinctive. In a single-enzyme disorder such as Hurler syndrome, the one enzyme is low everywhere. Here many enzymes are low inside the cells but high in plasma, pointing to a targeting defect rather than a catalytic one.

questions.q: 'Membrane transport proteins are the meeting point of physiology and pharmacology.' Discuss this statement by explaining how the asymmetric distribution of ions across the plasma membrane is established and maintained, and how drugs or diseases that disturb membrane transport produce clinical effects. Refer to at least three examples.
markScheme: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase: 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in per ATP; electrogenic; sets gradients
K⁺ leak channels make resting membrane potential approximate E_K; Nernst/GHK equations
Gradients drive secondary active transport (SGLT, Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger, Na⁺/H⁺ exchanger)
Membrane lipid bilayer impermeable to ions; channels and carriers give selectivity
Digoxin inhibits Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase: intracellular Na⁺ rises, NCX extrudes less Ca²⁺, SR loading and contractility increase; toxicity worse in hypokalaemia
SGLT2 inhibitors block proximal tubular glucose reabsorption: glycosuria, natriuresis; cardiorenal benefits
Proton pump inhibitors irreversibly block gastric H⁺/K⁺-ATPase
Cystic fibrosis: CFTR defect alters epithelial Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ and water transport
Hyperkalaemia and hypokalaemia alter E_K and cardiac excitability
Loop and thiazide diuretics inhibit NKCC2 and NCC respectively
Evaluation: shows transport proteins as central drug targets and disease sites; links molecular to clinical
questions.modelAnswer:
The lipid bilayer is almost impermeable to ions, so their distribution is set by proteins. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase hydrolyses one ATP to pump 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in. This keeps intracellular K⁺ near 140 mM and Na⁺ near 10–15 mM, and the net export of charge makes the pump slightly electrogenic. Resting membranes are mainly permeable to K⁺ through leak channels, so K⁺ diffuses out until the inside is negative enough to balance the chemical gradient. Resting potential therefore lies near E_K (about −90 mV), as the Nernst and Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz equations predict. The inward Na⁺ gradient is stored energy, which secondary active transporters use: SGLTs for glucose, the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger (NCX) for Ca²⁺ removal, and NHE for pH.

Disturbing these systems has clear clinical effects. Digoxin inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase in cardiac myocytes. Intracellular Na⁺ rises, the gradient driving NCX falls, and less Ca²⁺ is removed. The sarcoplasmic reticulum loads more Ca²⁺ and contraction strengthens. Digoxin competes with K⁺ at the pump, so hypokalaemia increases toxicity, which causes arrhythmias from Ca²⁺ overload.

SGLT2 inhibitors block Na⁺-coupled glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule. This causes glycosuria and mild natriuresis, and the drugs now have established roles in type 2 diabetes, heart failure and chronic kidney disease. Proton pump inhibitors irreversibly inactivate the gastric H⁺/K⁺-ATPase, while loop and thiazide diuretics inhibit NKCC2 and NCC.

Disease can strike the same machinery. In cystic fibrosis, loss of CFTR chloride and bicarbonate secretion dehydrates airway and pancreatic secretions. Potassium disorders shift E_K: hyperkalaemia depolarises cells and inactivates Na⁺ channels, while hypokalaemia hyperpolarises them and prolongs repolarisation, both predisposing to arrhythmia.

These examples show that transport proteins link molecular physiology to bedside medicine. They are among the most common drug targets, and their failure explains many disorders of excitability and epithelial function.

questions.q: Dr Kaur studies an enzyme with the following data, all at the same enzyme concentration. Without inhibitor: Km = 4 mM, Vmax = 200 µmol/min. With inhibitor X: apparent Km = 12 mM, Vmax = 200 µmol/min. With inhibitor Y: Km = 4 mM, Vmax = 100 µmol/min. (a) Calculate the reaction rate at [S] = 4 mM and at [S] = 12 mM under each condition. (b) Identify the type of inhibition shown by X and Y, and describe how each would appear on a Lineweaver–Burk plot. (c) Explain the clinical significance of competitive inhibition with reference to one named drug, and contrast it with irreversible inhibition.
markScheme: No inhibitor at 4 mM: v = 200 × 4/8 = 100 µmol/min
No inhibitor at 12 mM: v = 200 × 12/16 = 150 µmol/min
X is competitive (Km up, Vmax unchanged): lines intersect on the y-axis (same 1/Vmax), steeper slope
Y is non-competitive (Vmax down, Km unchanged): lines intersect on the x-axis (same −1/Km), higher y-intercept
Competitive inhibition can be overcome by raised substrate (X's effect shrinks proportionally at high [S])
Named example: methotrexate (DHFR) or statins (HMG-CoA reductase); folinic acid rescue bypasses methotrexate's block
Irreversible inhibitors (aspirin, organophosphates) need new enzyme synthesis for recovery; duration outlasts drug presence
Clear working and units
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Using v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]):
- No inhibitor: at 4 mM, v = 200 × 4/(4 + 4) = 100 µmol/min; at 12 mM, v = 200 × 12/16 = 150 µmol/min.
- Inhibitor X: at 4 mM, v = 200 × 4/(12 + 4) = 50 µmol/min; at 12 mM, v = 200 × 12/24 = 100 µmol/min.
- Inhibitor Y: at 4 mM, v = 100 × 4/8 = 50 µmol/min; at 12 mM, v = 100 × 12/16 = 75 µmol/min.

(b) X raises apparent Km threefold but leaves Vmax unchanged, so it is a competitive inhibitor. On a Lineweaver–Burk plot (1/v against 1/[S]), its line is steeper (slope Km/Vmax) but meets the uninhibited line at the same y-intercept, 1/Vmax = 0.005 min/µmol. Its x-intercept moves from −0.25 to about −0.083 mM⁻¹. Y halves Vmax without changing Km, the pattern of pure non-competitive inhibition. Its line has double the y-intercept (0.01), and the lines cross on the x-axis at −1/Km = −0.25 mM⁻¹. The data show the difference: going from 4 to 12 mM substrate, X's rate is 50% then 67% of uninhibited, but Y's stays at 50%. Extra substrate overcomes competitive inhibition but not non-competitive inhibition.

(c) Methotrexate is a structural analogue of folate. It binds dihydrofolate reductase very tightly and competitively, starving dividing cells of tetrahydrofolate for thymidylate and purine synthesis. Clinically, folinic acid rescue works by supplying reduced folate downstream of the block, not by out-competing at DHFR. Statins likewise compete with HMG-CoA at HMG-CoA reductase. In contrast, irreversible inhibitors bind covalently. Aspirin acetylates COX, and organophosphates phosphorylate acetylcholinesterase. Activity recovers only when new enzyme is made, so the effect outlasts the drug in plasma. This is why aspirin's antiplatelet effect lasts the lifespan of the platelet, about 7–10 days.

questions.q: Tomasz, a 24-year-old man of Mediterranean ancestry, develops dark urine, jaundice and fatigue three days after starting a course of an antimalarial for travel prophylaxis. Haemoglobin has fallen from 148 to 96 g/L; reticulocytes are raised; the blood film shows bite cells and, with supravital stain, Heinz bodies. Explain the biochemical basis of this presentation, linking the pentose phosphate pathway to red cell survival, and discuss how the diagnosis would be confirmed and managed.
markScheme: Likely diagnosis: G6PD deficiency (X-linked; males hemizygous) triggered by oxidant drug, e.g. primaquine
G6PD is rate-limiting enzyme of oxidative pentose phosphate pathway, generating NADPH
Red cells lack mitochondria; PPP is their only NADPH source
NADPH keeps glutathione reduced via glutathione reductase; GSH detoxifies H₂O₂ via glutathione peroxidase
Oxidant stress oxidises haemoglobin; denatured Hb precipitates as Heinz bodies; splenic macrophages remove them, creating bite cells
Intravascular and extravascular haemolysis: haemoglobinuria (dark urine), unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, reticulocytosis
Other triggers: fava beans, infection, dapsone, some sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, rasburicase
Confirm with G6PD enzyme assay, ideally after recovery as reticulocytes have higher activity (false normal during acute episode)
Management: stop trigger, supportive care, transfusion if severe, avoid oxidant drugs; test G6PD before primaquine/tafenoquine
Self-limiting because younger red cells have more enzyme
questions.modelAnswer:
The picture is acute haemolysis triggered by an oxidant drug in a man of Mediterranean ancestry. This is most consistent with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, an X-linked disorder, so males are hemizygous and fully affected. The 8-aminoquinoline antimalarials primaquine and tafenoquine are classic triggers.

G6PD catalyses the first, rate-limiting step of the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway, oxidising glucose-6-phosphate and reducing NADP⁺ to NADPH. Mature red cells have no mitochondria and no nucleus. The pentose phosphate pathway is their only source of NADPH, and they cannot replace enzyme that decays as the cell ages. NADPH drives glutathione reductase to keep glutathione in its reduced form (GSH), and glutathione peroxidase uses GSH to detoxify hydrogen peroxide and organic peroxides.

When G6PD activity is low, normal life is usually symptom-free. But an oxidant load from drugs, fava beans or infection overwhelms the cell. Haemoglobin sulphydryl groups are oxidised, and the denatured globin precipitates as Heinz bodies attached to the membrane. Membrane proteins and lipids are also damaged. Some cells lyse in the circulation, releasing haemoglobin that turns the urine dark. Others pass through the spleen, where macrophages remove the Heinz bodies, leaving bite cells, or destroy the whole cell. Haem breakdown raises unconjugated bilirubin, causing jaundice, and the marrow responds with reticulocytosis. The episode is usually self-limiting, because young red cells have more enzyme.

Diagnosis is confirmed by a quantitative G6PD assay. During acute haemolysis, the oldest and most deficient cells have already been destroyed and reticulocytes are enzyme-rich, so a test can be falsely normal; it should be repeated about three months later if suspicion remains. Management is to stop the trigger, give supportive care with hydration, and transfuse if anaemia is severe. Tomasz should be told which drugs and foods to avoid. G6PD status should be checked before prescribing primaquine or tafenoquine, and before other high-risk drugs such as rasburicase or dapsone.

questions.q: 'The regulation of glycolysis and gluconeogenesis is fundamentally about avoiding futile cycles.' Critically evaluate this statement, with reference to reciprocal enzyme control, hormonal signalling and tissue differences.
markScheme: Defines futile (substrate) cycle: simultaneous opposing irreversible reactions wasting ATP
Three bypass pairs: hexokinase/glucokinase vs G6Pase; PFK-1 vs FBPase-1; pyruvate kinase vs pyruvate carboxylase + PEPCK
Reciprocal allosteric control: fructose-2,6-bisphosphate activates PFK-1 and inhibits FBPase-1; AMP likewise; citrate and ATP inhibit PFK-1
Acetyl-CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase and inhibits PDH, diverting pyruvate to gluconeogenesis in fasting
Hormonal control: glucagon via cAMP/PKA phosphorylates PFK-2/FBPase-2 (lowering F2,6BP) and inactivates hepatic pyruvate kinase; insulin reverses
Transcriptional control: glucagon/cortisol induce PEPCK and G6Pase; insulin represses
Tissue differences: liver serves whole-body glucose; muscle lacks G6Pase and its isoforms respond to energy charge and adrenaline differently (muscle PFK-2 not inhibited by PKA)
Some cycling is useful: amplifies sensitivity of flux to effectors, and may generate heat (proposed in bumblebee flight muscle)
Cori cycle is an inter-organ cycle that costs ATP but serves a purpose (lactate recycling)
Evaluation: avoiding waste is one aim; the deeper purpose is matching flux to whole-body needs (glucose homeostasis) and energy charge
Clinical link: type 2 diabetes involves inappropriate hepatic gluconeogenesis; metformin reduces hepatic glucose output
Coherent argument and conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
A futile or substrate cycle occurs when two opposing, irreversible reactions run at the same time, with the net effect of hydrolysing ATP. Glycolysis and gluconeogenesis share seven reversible steps but differ at three points: glucokinase or hexokinase against glucose-6-phosphatase; PFK-1 against fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase; and pyruvate kinase against pyruvate carboxylase plus PEPCK. If all three pairs cycled freely, energy would leak away. The statement therefore captures something real.

The controls are reciprocal. Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate activates PFK-1 and inhibits FBPase-1; AMP acts in the same direction. ATP and citrate inhibit PFK-1. Acetyl-CoA from β-oxidation activates pyruvate carboxylase and inhibits PDH, steering pyruvate towards glucose during fasting. Hormones coordinate these switches in the liver. Glucagon raises cAMP, and PKA phosphorylates the bifunctional PFK-2/FBPase-2, lowering fructose-2,6-bisphosphate. PKA also inactivates hepatic pyruvate kinase. Insulin reverses these changes. Over hours, glucagon and cortisol induce PEPCK and glucose-6-phosphatase, and insulin represses them.

Calling this 'fundamentally' about futile cycles misses the main purpose, which is whole-body glucose homeostasis. The liver makes glucose for the brain and red cells during fasting, even while its own energy charge is high. Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase and expresses a PFK-2 isoform that PKA does not inhibit, so adrenaline speeds up glycolysis in muscle while slowing it in liver. These tissue differences show that the regulation is about distributing fuel between organs, not just saving ATP inside each cell.

Some cycling is also useful. A small amount of simultaneous flux makes net flux much more sensitive to small changes in effectors, amplifying control. Cycling at the PFK/FBPase step has also been proposed as a source of heat in bumblebee flight muscle. The Cori cycle between muscle and liver costs ATP overall but recycles lactate usefully.

Regulation also fails in disease. In type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance allows hepatic gluconeogenesis to continue inappropriately, and lowering hepatic glucose output is a major action of metformin.

Overall, preventing wasteful cycling is a necessary part of the design. The deeper aim is to match the direction and rate of flux to hormonal signals and the needs of each tissue. Controlled cycling is sometimes even used to sharpen that control.

questions.q: Ahmed, a 3-day-old boy born at term after an uneventful pregnancy, stops feeding, becomes drowsy and then has a seizure. He is tachypnoeic. Investigations: plasma ammonia 650 µmol/L (markedly raised), blood pH 7.48 with low pCO₂, plasma glucose normal, plasma citrulline low, plasma glutamine raised, and urinary orotic acid markedly raised. His maternal uncle died in the neonatal period of an unknown cause. Explain the most likely diagnosis with reference to the urea cycle, account for each investigation finding, and outline the principles of management.
markScheme: Diagnosis: ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency; X-linked (affected maternal uncle; mother likely carrier)
Urea cycle: CPS-I (needs N-acetylglutamate) and OTC in mitochondria; ASS, ASL, arginase in cytosol
OTC combines carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to form citrulline; deficiency lowers citrulline
Carbamoyl phosphate accumulates, leaves mitochondria, enters pyrimidine synthesis via cytosolic CAD, producing orotic acid
Ammonia accumulates; glutamine rises as glutamine synthetase buffers ammonia (contributing to astrocyte swelling and cerebral oedema)
Hyperammonaemia stimulates respiratory centre: respiratory alkalosis
Normal glucose and no ketoacidosis argue against organic acidaemia; distinguishes from CPS-I/NAGS deficiency where orotic acid is low
Presentation after protein feeding begins (day 2–3)
Management: emergency, stop protein, high-calorie glucose ± lipid to reverse catabolism
Nitrogen scavengers (sodium benzoate, sodium phenylbutyrate/phenylacetate) and arginine
Haemodialysis or haemofiltration for severe or refractory hyperammonaemia
Long-term: protein restriction, essential amino acids, scavengers, liver transplant in severe cases; genetic counselling and carrier testing of mother
questions.modelAnswer:
The most likely diagnosis is ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, the commonest urea cycle disorder. It is X-linked, which fits a severely affected male and a maternal uncle who died in the neonatal period; Ahmed's mother is probably a carrier.

The urea cycle in hepatocytes converts toxic ammonia into urea. In the mitochondria, carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (activated by N-acetylglutamate) combines NH₄⁺ and bicarbonate into carbamoyl phosphate, and OTC then joins it to ornithine to make citrulline. Citrulline is exported to the cytosol, where argininosuccinate synthetase, argininosuccinate lyase and arginase complete the cycle, releasing urea and regenerating ornithine.

Each finding follows from the block:
- Low citrulline: OTC is the enzyme that makes it.
- Raised orotic acid: unused carbamoyl phosphate leaks into the cytosol and enters pyrimidine synthesis beyond the usual control point (cytosolic CPS-II, part of CAD), so orotic acid accumulates. This separates OTC deficiency from CPS-I or NAGS deficiency, where orotic acid is normal or low.
- Very high ammonia and raised glutamine: glutamine synthetase traps ammonia as glutamine. In astrocytes this causes osmotic swelling and cerebral oedema, giving drowsiness and seizures.
- Tachypnoea with respiratory alkalosis (high pH, low pCO₂): ammonia stimulates the respiratory centre. This is typical of urea cycle defects, whereas organic acidaemias usually cause metabolic acidosis, often with ketosis.
- Timing: onset after two to three days reflects the start of protein feeding and neonatal catabolism.

Management is an emergency in a specialist metabolic centre. Protein is stopped temporarily, and high-energy intravenous glucose with lipid reverses catabolism. Nitrogen scavengers (sodium benzoate and sodium phenylacetate or phenylbutyrate) give alternative routes for nitrogen excretion, and arginine replaces what the broken cycle can no longer make. With ammonia at this level, rapid removal by haemodialysis or continuous haemofiltration is usually needed, because outcome depends on how long the brain is exposed. Long term, he will need a protein-restricted diet with essential amino acid supplements, oral scavengers and emergency regimens for illness, and liver transplantation may be considered. The family needs genetic counselling and carrier testing of his mother and female relatives.

questions.q: 'Familial hypercholesterolaemia is the clearest illustration of how understanding a single pathway can transform clinical practice.' Discuss, with reference to lipoprotein metabolism, receptor biology and therapeutic development.
markScheme: Lipoprotein overview: VLDL to IDL to LDL; apoB-100; LDL delivers cholesterol via LDL receptor
Brown and Goldstein's work on LDL receptor-mediated endocytosis (Nobel Prize 1985): clathrin-coated pits, receptor recycling, cholesterol-mediated feedback
SREBP-2 senses ER cholesterol; low sterol raises HMG-CoA reductase and LDLR transcription
FH genetics: autosomal dominant; LDLR (most), APOB, PCSK9 gain-of-function; heterozygous about 1 in 250; homozygous rare and severe
Clinical: raised LDL from birth, tendon xanthomata, corneal arcus, premature coronary disease; Simon Broome / Dutch Lipid Clinic criteria; cascade testing
Statins: HMG-CoA reductase inhibition up-regulates LDLR; need at least one functional allele for good response
Ezetimibe (NPC1L1), PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies and siRNA (inclisiran) increase LDLR recycling
Homozygous FH with null receptors responds poorly to LDLR-dependent drugs; lipoprotein apheresis, lomitapide (MTP inhibitor), evinacumab (ANGPTL3) act independently
PCSK9 loss-of-function variants with low LDL and less coronary disease validated the target (human genetics as drug discovery)
Evaluation: strong case, but other examples (BCR-ABL and imatinib, CFTR modulators) compete; FH remains underdiagnosed; polygenic hypercholesterolaemia common
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
The liver secretes triglyceride-rich VLDL carrying apoB-100. Lipoprotein lipase strips its triglyceride, leaving IDL and then cholesterol-rich LDL. Brown and Goldstein, who received the 1985 Nobel Prize, showed that LDL is cleared by a specific receptor. It clusters in clathrin-coated pits, is internalised, and releases its cargo in endosomes, after which the receptor recycles to the surface. Free cholesterol then switches off its own synthesis and uptake. The ER sensor SREBP-2 is retained when sterols are high and processed when they are low, increasing transcription of HMG-CoA reductase and the LDL receptor.

FH is autosomal dominant. Most cases involve LDLR, and others involve APOB (reduced receptor binding) or gain-of-function PCSK9 (increased receptor degradation). Heterozygous FH affects roughly 1 in 250 people. LDL is raised from birth, and patients develop tendon xanthomata and premature coronary disease. Homozygous FH is rare and can cause myocardial infarction in childhood. In the UK, NICE guidance supports diagnosis using the Simon Broome or Dutch Lipid Clinic criteria with genetic testing, followed by cascade testing of relatives.

Therapy follows the biology closely. Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, lowering hepatic cholesterol and activating SREBP-2, so more LDL receptors are made. They need at least one working LDLR allele. Ezetimibe reduces intestinal uptake through NPC1L1, with the same indirect effect on receptors. Human genetics then pointed to PCSK9: people with loss-of-function variants have lifelong low LDL and less coronary disease, which validated the target before drugs existed.
