PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies and the siRNA inclisiran followed. Patients with homozygous null receptors respond poorly to all these receptor-dependent drugs, which pushed the development of lomitapide (MTP inhibition), evinacumab (anti-ANGPTL3) and lipoprotein apheresis.

There are limits to the claim. Other examples rival it: imatinib for BCR-ABL and CFTR modulators also turned pathway biology into treatment. FH also remains widely underdiagnosed, and much hypercholesterolaemia is polygenic. Even so, FH is unusual: one discovery explained a disease, gave a mechanism for the most widely used class of cardiovascular drugs, and showed how human genetics can validate a drug target. That makes it perhaps the most complete example.

questions.q: Ruth, a 42-year-old woman, is diagnosed with colorectal cancer at the hepatic flexure. Her mother had endometrial cancer at 48 and her maternal uncle had colorectal cancer at 45. Immunohistochemistry on Ruth's tumour shows loss of MSH2 and MSH6 protein, and the tumour has high microsatellite instability. Explain the molecular basis of these findings, the pattern of inheritance, and the implications for Ruth's treatment and her relatives.
markScheme: Likely Lynch syndrome: germline mismatch repair (MMR) pathogenic variant, here MSH2 (MSH6 lost as its partner)
MMR corrects base mismatches and insertion-deletion loops from polymerase slippage, especially at microsatellites
MutSα (MSH2–MSH6) recognises errors; MutLα (MLH1–PMS2) excises; heterodimer partner degraded when MSH2 lost
Two-hit model: germline variant plus somatic inactivation in tumour cells
MMR deficiency causes accumulation of mutations, microsatellite instability, high tumour mutational burden
Autosomal dominant with high but incomplete penetrance; cancers at young age, right-sided colon, endometrium, ovary, upper urinary tract, small bowel, stomach
Distinguish from sporadic MLH1 promoter hypermethylation (typically MLH1/PMS2 loss, BRAF V600E)
Treatment: MMR-deficient tumours respond well to immune checkpoint inhibitors (neoantigen load); UK practice tests all colorectal cancers for MMR status (NICE DG27)
Relatives: genetic counselling, predictive testing, 50% risk to children and siblings
Surveillance: regular colonoscopy for carriers; aspirin chemoprevention (CAPP2 trial); consider risk-reducing hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy after childbearing
questions.modelAnswer:
Ruth's tumour has the features of Lynch syndrome. She has early-onset, right-sided colorectal cancer, a close family history of colorectal and endometrial cancer across generations, loss of MSH2 and MSH6 staining, and high microsatellite instability.

DNA mismatch repair fixes errors that escape polymerase proofreading. These are mainly single base mismatches and small loops formed when the polymerase slips on repetitive sequences (microsatellites). The MutSα heterodimer (MSH2–MSH6) recognises the error. MutLα (MLH1–PMS2) is then recruited, the newly made strand is cut, and the stretch is resynthesised. Partner proteins are unstable alone: when MSH2 is missing, MSH6 is degraded as well. Loss of both proteins on immunohistochemistry therefore points to an MSH2 defect, or less often an EPCAM deletion that silences MSH2.

In Lynch syndrome, every cell carries one pathogenic germline allele. A tumour forms when the second allele is lost somatically, following Knudson's two-hit model. Repair-deficient cells pile up mutations, especially frameshifts in microsatellites, including those in genes such as TGFBR2. The result is high MSI and a heavy load of neoantigens. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with high but incomplete penetrance, which fits affected relatives over two generations on the maternal side. Typical cancers are colorectal (often proximal), endometrial, ovarian, gastric, small bowel and upper urinary tract.

In the UK, NICE recommends MMR or MSI testing for every newly diagnosed colorectal cancer. This guards against confusion with sporadic MSI-high tumours, which usually show MLH1 and PMS2 loss from MLH1 promoter hypermethylation, often with BRAF V600E. Ruth should be referred for germline testing.

For treatment, MSI-high or MMR-deficient tumours respond well to immune checkpoint inhibitors because of their large neoantigen load. This is now standard practice in advanced disease and increasingly used earlier. MMR status also predicts a better stage-for-stage prognosis.

Her first-degree relatives each have a 50% chance of carrying the variant and should be offered genetic counselling and predictive testing. Carriers need regular colonoscopic surveillance. Daily aspirin reduces Lynch-associated cancers (CAPP2 trial). Women carriers should discuss risk-reducing hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy once their families are complete.

questions.q: 'Cancer is fundamentally a disease of disordered cell signalling.' Critically evaluate this statement with reference to oncogenes, tumour suppressors, cell-cycle control and targeted therapy.
markScheme: Hanahan and Weinberg hallmarks framework (2000, updated 2011, 2022) as structure
Oncogenes as gain-of-function signalling components: growth factor receptors (HER2 amplification, EGFR mutations), Ras, BRAF V600E, fusion kinases (BCR-ABL)
Tumour suppressors as signalling brakes: Rb (G1/S), p53 (DNA damage response), PTEN (opposes PI3K–Akt), APC (Wnt/β-catenin)
Cell-cycle control: cyclin D amplification, CDKN2A (p16) loss, CDK4/6 as drug target
Apoptosis evasion: BCL-2 overexpression in follicular lymphoma, t(14;18); venetoclax
Targeted therapy success validates signalling view: imatinib, trastuzumab, EGFR TKIs, BRAF/MEK inhibitors
Limits of targeted therapy: resistance through secondary mutations and bypass pathways
Not purely signalling: genome instability (MMR, BRCA), telomerase, metabolism (Warburg effect, IDH mutations), epigenetics
Tumour microenvironment, angiogenesis, immune evasion; checkpoint immunotherapy success relates to immunity not intrinsic signalling
Evolutionary/clonal view: cancer as somatic evolution; heterogeneity
Balanced conclusion: signalling is central and therapeutically powerful but insufficient as a complete account
Use of named examples and accurate mechanisms
questions.modelAnswer:
Much of cancer biology supports the statement. Oncogenes are mostly signalling components locked in the 'on' state:
- HER2 amplification in about 15–20% of breast cancers.
- Activating EGFR mutations in lung adenocarcinoma.
- KRAS mutations that impair GTP hydrolysis, so Ras stays active.
- BRAF V600E in melanoma, which keeps the MAPK pathway running.
- BCR-ABL in chronic myeloid leukaemia, a fusion kinase from t(9;22) that is constitutively active.

Many tumour suppressors are brakes on these pathways: PTEN opposes PI3K–Akt, APC degrades β-catenin, and NF1 inactivates Ras. Cell-cycle control is itself a signalling network. Cyclin D–CDK4/6 phosphorylates Rb, releasing E2F, and tumours escape through cyclin D amplification, loss of CDKN2A (p16) or loss of RB1. Evasion of apoptosis follows the same pattern: in follicular lymphoma, t(14;18) places BCL-2 under the immunoglobulin heavy-chain enhancer.

Targeted therapy is the strongest evidence for the signalling view. Imatinib transformed the outlook in CML. Trastuzumab, EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors, BRAF and MEK inhibitors, CDK4/6 inhibitors such as palbociclib, and the BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax all exploit dependence on a single pathway ('oncogene addiction').

But 'fundamentally' claims too much. Resistance through secondary kinase mutations or bypass pathways shows that cancer is an evolving cell population, not a fixed wiring fault. Genomic instability is a hallmark in its own right. BRCA-deficient homologous recombination and mismatch repair defects are caretaker failures, and they are treated through synthetic lethality with PARP inhibitors or through immunotherapy, not by blocking a pathway. Metabolic and epigenetic change (the Warburg effect, IDH oncometabolites) contribute too. Hanahan and Weinberg's updated hallmarks include angiogenesis, invasion, immune evasion and tumour-promoting inflammation, which depend on interactions with stroma and immune cells. The success of immune checkpoint inhibitors, especially in tumours with many mutations, works through T-cell immunity rather than by correcting signalling inside the tumour.

In conclusion, disordered signalling is a central and highly druggable part of cancer, and it explains why many targeted drugs work. A complete account must also include genomic instability, clonal evolution, metabolism and the tumour microenvironment. Cancer is better described as somatic evolution in which signalling is one of several key drivers.

questions.q: Kofi, a 30-year-old aid worker, returns from a cholera outbreak area. Within a day he has passed many litres of painless, pale 'rice-water' stool without blood. He is tachycardic and hypotensive, with dry mucous membranes. Bloods show hypokalaemia and a low bicarbonate. Stool microscopy shows no leucocytes. Explain how cholera toxin disrupts G protein signalling to produce these findings, why oral rehydration solution works, and how the mechanism of pertussis toxin differs.
markScheme: G protein cycle: GPCR activation causes GDP/GTP exchange on Gα; Gα-GTP dissociates and acts; intrinsic GTPase terminates signal
Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase raising cAMP; Gi inhibits it
Cholera toxin is an AB5 toxin; B subunits bind GM1 ganglioside; A1 fragment ADP-ribosylates Gsα (arginine)
This abolishes GTPase activity, so Gsα stays active and adenylyl cyclase is persistently stimulated
Raised cAMP activates PKA, which phosphorylates and opens CFTR, causing chloride secretion; NHE3-mediated Na⁺ absorption is inhibited
Water follows osmotically: profuse 'rice-water' diarrhoea, dehydration, hypokalaemia, metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate loss)
Mucosa intact: no inflammation; SGLT1 Na⁺-glucose co-transport preserved, the basis for oral rehydration solution
Pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates Gi (cysteine), preventing coupling to receptor, so Gi cannot inhibit adenylyl cyclase; cAMP rises
Contrast: cholera activates a stimulator; pertussis disables an inhibitor
questions.modelAnswer:
Heterotrimeric G proteins act as timed switches. When a ligand activates a G protein-coupled receptor, the Gα subunit exchanges GDP for GTP and separates from Gβγ to act on its effectors. Its intrinsic GTPase then hydrolyses GTP, ending the signal. Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase, and Gi inhibits it.

Cholera toxin is an AB5 toxin. Its B pentamer binds GM1 ganglioside on enterocytes, and after retrograde transport the A1 fragment reaches the cytosol. There it ADP-ribosylates an arginine on Gsα, abolishing its GTPase activity. Gsα stays GTP-bound, adenylyl cyclase runs continuously, and cAMP rises. PKA phosphorylates CFTR in crypt cells, driving large-scale secretion of chloride, with sodium and water following. Raised cAMP also inhibits NaCl absorption through the Na⁺/H⁺ exchanger NHE3 in villus cells.

The clinical features follow from this. The result is a massive, painless, watery 'rice-water' diarrhoea that can reach many litres a day, causing hypovolaemic shock, hypokalaemia and metabolic acidosis from bicarbonate loss. The mucosa stays structurally intact, so there is no blood and little inflammation. Na⁺–glucose co-transport through SGLT1 still works. Oral rehydration solution exploits this: glucose drives sodium, and therefore water, absorption despite the secretory state.

Pertussis toxin, also an AB5 toxin, ADP-ribosylates a cysteine on Giα. Gi can then no longer couple to its receptors and stays inactive in the GDP-bound form. The inhibitory brake on adenylyl cyclase is lost, so cAMP rises in target cells such as airway cells and leucocytes. This contributes to the lymphocytosis and other systemic effects of whooping cough. Both toxins raise cAMP but by opposite routes: cholera toxin keeps the stimulator switched on, while pertussis toxin disables the inhibitor.

questions.q: Sophie, aged 28, is referred to clinical genetics. Her brother had Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Her parents are unaffected and her mother's creatine kinase is raised. Sophie's partner has no family history. (a) Draw on inheritance principles to explain the risk that Sophie is a carrier, given that her mother is presumed a carrier, and the risk to her future children. (b) Explain why some female carriers develop symptoms. (c) Discuss the molecular basis of Duchenne versus Becker muscular dystrophy and outline the genetic testing available to Sophie.
markScheme: DMD: X-linked recessive; DMD gene on Xp21, encodes dystrophin, one of the largest human genes
If mother is a carrier, Sophie's prior carrier risk is 1/2
If Sophie is a carrier: each son 1/2 affected; each daughter 1/2 carrier
Overall prior risk of an affected son = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 per son; 1/8 per pregnancy of unknown sex
Note that about a third of isolated cases arise de novo and gonadal mosaicism can occur, so maternal carrier status should be confirmed
Manifesting carriers: skewed X-inactivation (lyonisation) favouring the mutant X; can cause weakness or cardiomyopathy; carriers need cardiac surveillance
Reading-frame rule: out-of-frame deletions/duplications or nonsense variants cause absent dystrophin (Duchenne); in-frame deletions give truncated partly functional dystrophin (Becker)
Dystrophin links actin cytoskeleton to dystroglycan complex; loss causes membrane fragility and fibre necrosis
Testing: identify familial variant (MLPA for deletions/duplications, sequencing for point variants); then targeted carrier testing for Sophie
Reproductive options: prenatal diagnosis (CVS or amniocentesis), non-invasive fetal sexing, PGT-M, donor gametes; genetic counselling throughout
Correct probability working
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Duchenne muscular dystrophy is X-linked recessive and caused by variants in DMD on Xp21, which encodes dystrophin. If Sophie's mother is a carrier (X^D X^d), each daughter has a 1/2 chance of inheriting the mutant X. Sophie's prior carrier risk is therefore 1/2. If she is a carrier and her partner is unaffected, each son has a 1/2 chance of being affected and each daughter a 1/2 chance of being a carrier. Before testing, her risk of an affected son is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 for each son, or 1/8 for any pregnancy of unknown sex. About a third of isolated DMD cases arise de novo, so the mother's status should be confirmed molecularly. A raised CK supports carrier status but a normal CK does not exclude it. Gonadal mosaicism means recurrence is possible even if her blood test is negative.

(b) In females, one X is randomly inactivated early in development (lyonisation). If inactivation is skewed so that the normal X is silenced in most muscle cells, a carrier can develop proximal weakness, cramps or, importantly, dilated cardiomyopathy. Carriers are therefore offered cardiac assessment. 

(c) Dystrophin links the actin cytoskeleton, through the dystroglycan complex, to the extracellular matrix, and it stabilises the sarcolemma during contraction. Under the reading-frame rule, deletions or duplications that disrupt the frame, and nonsense variants, cause premature termination and absent dystrophin. This gives Duchenne disease, with onset in early childhood and loss of walking typically by the early teens. In-frame deletions keep a shortened but partly functional protein, giving the milder Becker phenotype. Exon-skipping therapy aims to restore the frame.

Testing should first identify the familial variant in her brother or mother. MLPA detects the exon deletions and duplications behind most cases, and sequencing finds point variants. Sophie can then have targeted carrier testing. If she is a carrier, her options include prenatal diagnosis by chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis (with earlier non-invasive fetal sexing from cell-free DNA), preimplantation genetic testing (PGT-M) or donor gametes, all with genetic counselling.

questions.q: 'Mendelian inheritance is the exception, not the rule, in human disease.' Discuss with reference to non-classical inheritance mechanisms and multifactorial disease.
markScheme: Mendelian disorders are individually rare but collectively significant; clear patterns (AD, AR, XL)
Even Mendelian conditions show incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity (BRCA1/2, NF1), modifiers (CFTR genotype-phenotype variability)
Repeat expansions and anticipation: Huntington (CAG), myotonic dystrophy type 1, fragile X; parent-of-origin effects
Genomic imprinting: Prader–Willi/Angelman (15q11–q13); uniparental disomy
Mitochondrial inheritance: maternal, heteroplasmy, threshold effect
Mosaicism (somatic and gonadal); de novo variants as major cause of severe developmental disorders (Deciphering Developmental Disorders study)
Digenic and oligogenic inheritance examples (e.g. some retinitis pigmentosa)
Multifactorial diseases (coronary disease, type 2 diabetes, schizophrenia): liability-threshold model, heritability, GWAS identify many small-effect variants, polygenic risk scores
Environment and gene-environment interaction; epigenetics
Continuum: monogenic forms within common diseases (FH, MODY) and polygenic modifiers of monogenic disease penetrance
Clinical implications: genomic medicine, NHS Genomic Medicine Service; limits of polygenic risk scores
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Mendel's laws describe single-locus traits that segregate predictably. In human disease, autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive and X-linked patterns explain thousands of conditions, such as cystic fibrosis, Huntington disease and haemophilia. Each is rare, but together they matter. Whether they are 'the exception' depends on whether we count conditions or disease burden.

Even classic Mendelian disorders often break the simple rules. Penetrance may be incomplete (BRCA1/2) and expressivity variable (NF1). Genetic modifiers and environment shape severity, as in cystic fibrosis lung disease, which differs between siblings with the same CFTR genotype. Several mechanisms depart further from classical patterns:
- Unstable repeat expansions cause anticipation, with parent-of-origin effects: paternal expansion in Huntington disease, the maternal congenital form of myotonic dystrophy, and maternal expansion in fragile X.
- Genomic imprinting means the same 15q11–q13 deletion causes Prader–Willi syndrome if paternal and Angelman syndrome if maternal; uniparental disomy can mimic either.
- Mitochondrial disease passes only through the mother, and heteroplasmy and threshold effects make severity unpredictable.
- Somatic and gonadal mosaicism, together with de novo variants, account for many severe developmental disorders. Large studies such as Deciphering Developmental Disorders have shown this.

Most of the disease burden is multifactorial: coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes, asthma and schizophrenia. The liability-threshold model treats risk as a continuous trait shaped by many variants of small effect and by environment, with disease appearing above a threshold. Genome-wide association studies have found hundreds of loci, which polygenic risk scores combine; these predict modestly and less accurately in people of non-European ancestry.

Single-gene and complex disease form a spectrum rather than two separate groups. Common diseases contain monogenic subsets, such as familial hypercholesterolaemia in coronary disease and MODY in diabetes. Polygenic background also modifies the penetrance of monogenic variants.

In conclusion, if 'rule' means the main cause of disease in the population, the statement is largely correct: most disease burden is multifactorial. But Mendelian disorders remain clinically important, and studying them reveals biological pathways, from the LDL receptor to CFTR. Genomic medicine needs both models.
